Thoth. The ibis-headed god of wisdom, writing, and cosmic order in Egyptian mythology. He embodied the idea that the word, spoken and written, possesses creative and binding power. Thoth served as the divine scribe and record-keeper of the gods themselves and was essential not only to the gods' maintenance of the cosmos but to human civilization itself. Thoth invented writing and all forms of communication, and Egyptians credited him with the sacred knowledge that sustained both the universe and the possibility of an afterlife. The ibis was sacred to him for its curved beak, which resembled the crescent moon. He was depicted as an ibis-headed deity, though also depicted in some contexts as a baboon, particularly in scenes of greeting the sun. He was often shown wearing the lunar crescent and disk, associating him with the moon's cycles and nocturnal wisdom. He represented the principle of divine intelligence and the power of spoken and written language to shape reality. Thoth invented writing, specifically hieroglyphics, and all forms of communication and speech. Egyptians called their script the language of Thoth, recognizing his role as the originator of written language itself. As the divine scribe, he recorded the deeds of gods and humans, maintaining the cosmic record and preserving divine knowledge for eternity. He was the god of wisdom, magic known as heka, mathematics, astronomy, medicine, and all learned arts. He was the patron of scribes, scholars, and priests, guiding all who sought knowledge and truth. As keeper of the Book of the Dead, Thoth maintained the funerary texts that guided souls through the many perils of the underworld, the Duat, toward eternal life with Osiris. His true name and the power of his words were believed to grant access to divine knowledge and the deepest secrets of resurrection. He served as a divine judge who recorded the judgment of souls in the afterlife, weighing their hearts against Ma'at's feather of truth at the cosmic scales. Associated with the moon and its cycles, Thoth served as the regulator of time, seasons, and the rhythms that governed the cosmos. His baboon form was believed to greet the rising sun each dawn, celebrating Ra's nightly victory over the chaos serpent Apophis. He served as a judge and mediator between conflicting gods, including the prolonged dispute between Horus and Set over the Egyptian throne and the right to rule. Unlike gods who ruled through force or divine lineage, Thoth's authority derived from knowledge and the power of the word. This made him especially important in Egyptian civilization, where writing and scribal practice were central to maintaining social order and divine knowledge. In later Hellenistic times, when Greeks encountered Egyptian culture, Thoth was syncretized with Hermes, the Greek messenger god, and the fusion became Hermes Trismegistus, Thrice-Great Hermes, the legendary founder of Hermeticism and Western occult tradition. Medieval and Renaissance alchemists attributed profound mystical texts to Hermes Trismegistus, treating Thoth's association with secret knowledge as a supreme authority on hidden wisdom. His role as the scribe of the gods influenced countless mythologies' depictions of wisdom figures who record and judge the deeds of gods and humans.
